t: Frog Position After T Seconds — Editorial
o: The frog walks down a tree from vertex 1, at each step choosing uniformly among its unvisited neighbors (its children, since it can't go back). It must be exactly on `target` after `t` seconds, or stuck there forever if it arrived early and has no children. So the answer is the product of branching probabilities along the root-to-target path, but only if the path length equals `t`, or is less than `t` while target is a leaf. In Example 1, the path 1→2→4 has length 2 = t, probability 1/3 · 1/2 = 1/6. In Example 2, path 1→7 has length 1 = t, probability 1/3. With n ≤ 100 and t ≤ 50, a simple BFS/DFS over the tree tracking depth and accumulated probability is more than sufficient.
k: Since the graph is a tree rooted at vertex 1, each node's unvisited neighbors are exactly its children; the frog's path to any node is unique.
The answer is nonzero only when the distance from 1 to target equals t, or is strictly less than t and target is a leaf.
The probability of reaching a node is the product of 1/(number of children) along the path from the root.

a.i: Run BFS from vertex 1 carrying (node, time, probability). At each node compute the number of children (neighbors excluding the parent). If we reach target: return the probability if time == t, or if time < t and target has no children; otherwise 0. If BFS finishes without visiting target in time, return 0.
s: Build an adjacency list from edges.
BFS from vertex 1 storing (node, parent, elapsed time, probability so far).
For each dequeued node, count children = degree − 1 (degree for root).
If node == target: return prob if time == t, or time < t and no children; else 0.
Otherwise push each child with prob / childCount and time + 1, if time < t.
a.t: O(n) — each vertex is enqueued once and adjacency scans are linear in tree size.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency list plus BFS queue.

a.i: Recursively walk from the root toward target, multiplying probabilities by 1/(number of children) at each step. When we reach target, check the timing condition: depth == t, or depth < t and target is a leaf. This avoids processing the whole tree level by level and expresses the logic very directly.
s: Build adjacency list; run DFS(1, parent=0, depth=0, prob=1.0).
Count children of current node (neighbors other than parent).
If node == target: return prob if depth == t or (depth < t and no children), else 0.
If depth >= t, stop descending; otherwise recurse into each child with prob / childCount.
Return 0 if target never reached within the explored subtree.
a.t: O(n) — visits each vertex at most once along tree paths.
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency list plus recursion stack up to tree height O(n).

w: In an interview, lead with the key observation that a tree gives a unique root-to-target path, making the probability a simple product of branching factors — then either BFS or DFS works; DFS is slightly cleaner. Common pitfalls: forgetting the 'arrived early and stuck on a leaf' case (target reached before t with no children still counts); forgetting that arriving before t at a non-leaf means probability 0; mishandling the root's child count (no parent, so all neighbors are children); and treating the graph as having cycles. Edge cases: target == 1 (answer is 1 iff t... actually always 1, since the frog starts there and can only stay if it has no unvisited moves — note with n=1 the answer is 1 for any t). Follow-ups might ask for the probability distribution over all vertices after t seconds, which the same traversal computes in one pass.
